english_transcription:
Oded Napchi: Okay, so we will try to discuss the case study of Metaverse, the company that I'm managing now. I will also show you our system, and I will also try to discuss with you the challenges — maybe you will have good ideas for us. So let's start.

Usually I like to regard startups as some kind of a telenovela. It's always a story where someone loved something, then was betrayed, then loved another, and then they discovered the long-lost daughter had disappeared. Yes, this is basically startups.

In our case, the origin story of our startup actually started as a division of another company. There was a company called AllSeated that Forbes said invented the Metaverse, and they raised a lot of money. The basic business was designing events — let's say you want to do a bar mitzvah, you come to this company, they show you the space, and you can choose which kind of table, chair, or whatever you want in the venue. But then COVID came, and all the event organizer companies came to them and said, "Hey, you already have 3D models of our venues and you're working with us — let's do a virtual event." This is when the company boomed. Forbes said it invented the Metaverse before Mark Zuckerberg, and they raised $20 million without any challenge, and life was very good.

But then COVID ended. So it was clear to them that they couldn't continue doing the same thing, and they decided to spin out the company. Why? Because by the time they announced the split and started negotiating with potential customers, within a few months they had gathered 15 paying customers.

So when I arrived, they came to me and said, "Hey, we have 15 paying customers — some of them are Fortune 500: Simmons, Citizens Bank, and Ferrero. And we have dozens of customers in the pipeline, but we don't really understand why they are customers of ours." It's a really strange thing to say to someone, especially when you're interviewing to be CEO. I asked them, "Okay, what is your positioning?" They said, "We are an enterprise Metaverse." And what is your USP? "You don't need to install anything, you don't need a VR headset, and we use video streaming instead of avatars."

So I did a quick search — the way I analyze these things. I checked how many people are interested in "enterprise Metaverse," how many people search for it. About 20 searches a year, more or less, even now. By the way, everyone who searches for "enterprise Metaverse" — I get them. I have an 80% conversion rate. That means if someone searches for it, they'll probably become a client. But I spend $35 a month on it. That's it.

So what did I do? I actually did what Jonathan talked about: I ranked the customers and asked them, in a naturally intelligent way, "Why do you like us?" And I noticed something. But first — just as Jonathan said, product is nice, but marketing is king. If you have a mediocre product but good marketing, you will be a success. If you have the greatest product ever made but mediocre marketing, nothing will happen. I can tell you, after two startups and two big communication companies in Israel — this is the story. Good ideas? You get them a dime a dozen. Good marketing ideas? I've been interviewing the best marketers in the country for over a month and we're still struggling, but we have a solution. Okay.

So another way for me to analyze a company's potential success is to look at the nuts and bolts of the marketing. They had PPC marketing — what Jonathan likes to call "brute force," and for all the right reasons. They spent about $7,500 a month and got about one customer every two months. That means the customer acquisition cost was about $12,000, and the profit per customer was $20,000 — which is good, but not much. One customer every two months when you're spending that much money is a problem.

Then there was ABM. I don't know if you've discussed it here — ABM is the buzzword now. It's basically cold calls with a sophisticated name. And cold calls — what's nice is they apparently don't cost you any advertising budget, right? But you do have personnel costs, so it actually came to $16,000. They got over 100 leads per month, which is very nice — but one customer in a year. Total failure. The first thing I did was let go of all the ABM people. Five people were cut from the company.

And here's something I hadn't noticed at the beginning: they had six customers that came almost entirely from business development. I hadn't taken that into consideration. That's a hint — a spoiler for later.

So, as I said: not enough leads, a very long sales cycle of over half a year, and the minimum requirements from customers were very high. Because when you're working with enterprise solutions, you need to be totally safe, totally solid. And I can tell you from 20 years of experience — going after enterprise customers when you're just starting out will probably kill your company. It's like trying to eat a fish that's too big. It's a total mistake.

So I started interviewing the customers. Fifteen customers — I could interview them quite easily. I noticed that the two biggest ones were doing training. And I even understood it's not just training — they also call it "learning and development" and "organizational development." Nice. Also, five of my mid-size customers were in the same category. So the majority of customers, and the highest-yielding ones, were in training and learning and development.

So I thought, okay, I found the use case: HR divisions doing training. And then I interviewed them and asked, "Why do you like us so much?" They told me something very interesting. Their biggest problem was people leaving the company very fast — they invest a lot of time in recruiting and training, and then three months after onboarding, the employee leaves. It's a huge problem. But they found that if, during the onboarding process, the new employee speaks with other employees, the chance that they'll leave drops significantly. And it makes sense — if you have a friend at your workplace, you don't leave. So they said, "In your system, people talk a lot. We hit the benchmark. We have a lot of communication. We're doing a good job."

Great. And then I used this insight: 12 billion working days are lost every year due to employee burnout and turnover, costing a trillion dollars annually. We have a solution: connection between people. And when I looked at the marketing with this new positioning, the customer acquisition cost dropped to $2,500 — a third of the previous amount. Our average revenue per customer stayed more or less the same as before. We cut the budget to a third, doubled the results, and the sales cycle came down to two months — very reasonable. We're currently speaking about a year's worth of data, because the company has only existed for one year, so it's hard to do much more with it.

But what's the problem? We went from 10 searches to 100 searches — but we still can't build a business on that. The conversion rate is more reasonable now, about 10%, which means I get about 10 leads per month and can grow to two or three customers a month. That's not a real business yet. At the same time, I still need to do a lot of security and compliance testing, I still need a customer success team to manage them, and customers usually want a one-time event, not an ongoing activity.

And the thing that troubled me most — and I think Jonathan didn't mention this — investors weren't interested. And we always have to remember: we're not only marketing to the market, we're also marketing to investors. And as a founder — you might not like to hear this, Jonathan — the majority of your work is marketing to investors. If you're lucky, the investor is professional and intelligent, and your marketing to the investor will also be relevant for the market. But it's not always like that.

So I come in and say, "HR divisions have money." They say, "We know they don't — we've invested before and lost, so we're not going there. And that's it." You can't do anything at that point. I can't show them that HR actually drives business outcomes — they already have a preconception. A good example: this was the answer I got from Pitango and UpWest — legitimate, top-tier VCs.

Student: Can I ask — it seems like your ICP was actually defined by the customers themselves?

Oded Napchi: A little bit, yes. Again, I would say there's no standard way of building a startup. In my case, I joined a startup that was almost a year old and was asked to move it forward. Most of the projects I take on are like this — when I say I "founded" something, in many cases I was asked to come in at the founder level and do a pivot. My biggest success was a hero video advertising company that lasted 15 years. When I first joined, it was a DRM company — not connected at all — but when I understood who was interested, and why, and where it could go, I took it in that direction.

So now let's take a short break — I've explained the problem, and I want to show you the system. Then we'll discuss it a bit and I'll give you an example of the direction I want to take the company now.

[Demo begins]

So this is our environment — I built this one specifically for this demo. Let me find a view that gives you a nice look at it. Basically, what you can see here is a 3D environment that gives a realistic feeling. There are people walking around, and when I click on someone, it opens a video stream so I can communicate with them. So it's not like Zoom, where you're forced to be in a room with everyone — you can choose with whom you want to speak, where you want to speak, and why you want to speak.

Student: How much does it cost to build such an environment, in terms of expenses?

Oded Napchi: The real cost — not what I charge, but what it costs me — is about $1 per user.

Student: But you have to build the environment itself.

Oded Napchi: Yeah, but building the environment — here's the nice trick: most environments are pre-built as templates, and then I just make small alterations. So the cost of building an environment is almost trivial. I do charge for it, but it's almost no cost for me.

Student: But I mean the environment itself — it's a real physical space?

Oded Napchi: It's a 3D space. Yes.

Student: How many hours do you spend building one?

Oded Napchi: A completely new environment like this one — two hours.

Student: So if I come to you — for example, I have a venue in Savion and I'd like to sell — I could ask you to build my villa in this environment?
I charge for this. Yes, but it actually has almost no cost for me.

No, I mean the environment — it's a real space.

It's a 3D space. Yeah.

How many hours do you spend building it?

A whole new environment — like this specific environment — two hours.

So if I'll go to you, for example, I have a villa in Savion. I'd like to sell it. I'll ask you to build my villa in this environment.

So if it is something very specific — again, our main business, although I have one customer who is in real estate. Now most of our customers use it, as I mentioned, for training, conferences, and things like this. And most of the spaces are more or less the same. If you want me to build you a specific house, it might take me a day. It depends how accurate you want it to be, because if you want it to be really accurate, I need to bring a team and do 3D measurement with lasers and so on. I don't think that ever happened to us. I even built once — I was commissioned to build Herod's Temple. It took us a couple of hours. Why?

Because you have so many models of Herod's Temple that you don't need to invest much.

Yeah. But if somebody really wants to sell their property —

Yeah, we have one.

This property costs, for example, $10 million.

Even if it costs a lot of money, it will be hundreds of dollars. I have one customer, a big real estate company from Switzerland, and they pay us like $1,000 a month and they get quite a lot. So it costs much less than it is perceived to cost. The problem is that the biggest cost for us is training the people to operate the system. And that's a big problem. Yeah.

So if I go near one of the people in this metaverse, I can hear their conversation?

Yeah, it's proximity-based. And by the way, if I go to — I'll show you a video of one of our events — it starts working as I get closer. And this is how an actual event looks. You see a lot of people, you have the main stage. When you enter the main stage, the CEO is speaking, so it changes to something a little bit like Zoom — you're not bothering anyone. Nutella is one of our biggest customers, and they just renewed their license again.

Do you have customers that use it as a virtual office?

I think I won't show you much more than this. We have the use cases here and so on. If you want, I can show you an actual space of a real customer and how it looks. This is a real customer — you won't see people now because the event is closed. It's a big bank from Canada, and their idea was that every salesperson is a rock star. So they built it as a rock arena. They have a merchandise shop, a bounty game you can play, and the main event stage — nice and interesting.

But now, after you've seen this, we try to take a Jonathan-style approach to how to build startups — which, again, I strongly agree with.

We try to think: what will be our beachhead? What is the one solution we can say will make everybody interested in the company? When I think about it — targeting HR departments, doing a webinar about HR — I have several well-known HR people I thought about bringing in, but it didn't feel like enough. And we don't think it's a big enough market. So I try to think: let's find the general case, of which training is a specific instance. Do you follow the logic? Let's think that training is an example of a much bigger use case.

In the beginning, the company thought it was Enterprise Metaverse, but we understood there is no market. And, going to one of the questions here, in Enterprise Metaverse you also have office spaces and conferences — and they simply don't work. So what is the use case?

What I did this time was go to industry experts — not customers — because the imagination of customers is limited. They know what they've tried; they don't know what they've never tried. So if I want something visionary, I need to come at it from a different angle. I went to industry experts — people who were senior at Zoom, Teams, ON24, and so on. They told me: the general space is long sessions with high engagement. Why? Because Zoom, Teams, and all the other platforms lose engagement after 40 minutes. All of them will tell you: you cannot have a session longer than 40 minutes.

But there are many cases where you need a session longer than 40 minutes. Training is one of them, onboarding is one of them — but you also have e-learning, medical, and many other use cases. There is actually a very big need for longer sessions, and there's a big market for this.

We then tried to think: what is our product's USP in this space? So this is our messaging, and you can put it simply: 75% of video conference users lose engagement after 60 minutes. Metaverse keeps them engaged for over 3 hours. A very simple message that resonates with everybody, because everybody is trying to run a long session and everybody knows it's relatively hard.

I also tried to understand why our engagement is higher. I'm doing a PhD in philosophy of knowledge, and engagement is part of knowledge. So I knew that if I enable people to decide what they want to do, they will have higher engagement. I knew that if I enable interactions, people will have higher engagement. Education is a social activity — if I let people discuss with each other, they will have higher engagement. And there's a longer list of reasons.

So I mentioned who needs a longer session: webinars, virtual events, sales events, job interviews, onboarding. And then we needed to think about who our potential customer would be. We had a nice insight here: we learned that in big companies — which were our original customers — it's their events division. But when you go to smaller companies, you discover that they use content marketing agencies. And it's a big segment — in the US there are over 20,000 content marketing agencies.

So now I think I know what my market is and what the problem of that market is. The market is content marketing agencies. The problem is that when they try to run longer events, engagement drops. When I started calling content marketing agencies, they said: what a coincidence — last week we had a customer who wanted exactly this kind of product, and we told them it doesn't exist. We told them a webinar of over an hour is like a unicorn.

So at this point I want to stop for a moment before I tell you what direction we're heading in as we try to find the beachhead and the marketing engine. After everything you've heard from Jonathan's lectures, it will be interesting for me to hear your thoughts: what would you do to create a beachhead and infiltrate the market in the space of long sessions with high engagement, targeting content marketing agencies?

Why not telemedicine in healthcare?

First, there's no strong reason to. Second — yeah, I know telemedicine. I want to reduce the number of approvals I need to get for each system. My intuition tells me that medical care will require a lot of preparation — cybersecurity and so on. But there is another segment in medical that we are working on.

What if they pay more? You can charge $2,000, you can charge $20,000.

No, but again, when you're speaking about medical devices, the use case would still probably be conference, webinar, or training.

No, I'm thinking — for example, you want to consult an expert from the US. I think it's much more logical to meet in this kind of platform, like a more immersive version of Zoom. You'd probably need to adjust it a bit — for example, you're going to show some visuals — but you're not talking about the target audience.

I'm talking about the marketing engine. What I mean is: what acquisition strategy should I use so that someone will become interested in us? Because as Jonathan said — yes, we can do PPC. I'll show you the PPC results in a moment; they're good. We can do PPC, LinkedIn, webinars, content marketing. We're doing all of it. That's fine. But that's brute force — we need to find the elegant solution. That's what I'm trying to figure out. It's a very creative challenge.

What about schools and universities?

Again, that's a target audience, not a marketing engine. All the target audiences you've mentioned are very good. But the reason I think we should go to content marketing agencies rather than, say, psychological sessions — let me just explain what Odette is asking.

When we built ZoomInfo, we built a directory of all the people in our database. So if anyone went online, didn't know anything about us, and typed in "Jonathan Stern," the ZoomInfo page would jump to the top of the list. They'd click on it and say, "What is ZoomInfo?" — and that's how we reached millions of people. That's essentially the question being asked here: is there any magic like that, which will make people encounter the metaverse and say, "Wow, this is really cool, I can use this"? That's the question.

And then let me give another example I like. DocuSign had a very nice engine. Every time you used DocuSign, it showed you in a calculator how many trees you saved — and they notified both sides. So you know you want to save trees, and it was a very compelling message. There are many companies that do this. I also like what Daniel is doing as a promotion. Did you already discuss this? Who else mentioned entertainment?

Yeah, what about entertainment? People spend tons of time in front of screens — all kinds of screens — watching reality shows like Big Brother or whatever. If you can create a metaverse that provides entertainment to a broad audience —

I'll give you an example of an idea based on your insight. Remember, the objective of this game — let's call it that — is to bring us more customers from the segments we've defined. So going with your rationale: gaming, a virtual casino, playing together. But then that means my use case becomes gambling.

What I actually thought — which is a little bit like what you said — is: who are the people working at content marketing agencies? At the end of the day, we're working with people. In very general terms, they're between 25 and 35, college-educated, probably living in big cities. Those are the people we're working with.

So I said: what media are they consuming? The most popular medium today for this age group is video games. I looked at which games are most successful for this segment and found ten. Then I went to Reddit, looked for those communities, and found that each one of those games has more than 100,000 people in its subreddit. So maybe I can host an event for one of those gaming communities inside our metaverse — and through that, get a nice portion of potential customers visiting our environment.
er games. So I looked at which computer games are the most successful for this segment. I found 10. So I went to Reddit and looked for the community, and I found that each one of these games has more than 100,000 people in the Reddit community. So maybe I can do an event for the community of the game in our metaverse, and then we'll get a nice portion of potential customers visiting my environment.

Not expecting that I'm doing a sale on them, because one of the biggest problems with this audience is that they are very sales-reluctant — they can feel when you're going to sell them something. I'll jump a little bit and tell you what our idea is, and I'd love your thoughts on it. So what I said is that I checked it about brute-force engagement. It's a popular term. "Engagement" — ideas on how to increase engagement in Zoom. A nice bunch of terms, over 600 in a month, which means I'm starting to get into normal numbers. I don't have yet what my customer acquisition cost is, or even what my cost per lead is, because we started just two weeks ago and we're still testing — but it shows potential. But it's a brute force approach, and we are not here for this.

So what we said is: let's take ownership of the term "engagement." Let's try to position ourselves as the engagement company. Why? Remember, we want to sell long sessions with high engagement. So if I take ownership of the term "engagement," it helps — it could help. How do you take ownership? The first phase that we want to do — something we're doing in any case — is establish ourselves as thought leaders: publish articles, webinars, posts. If any one of you searches for me, you'll see that I publish posts about engagement on every platform known to humankind — Bluesky, Twitter, Threads, Reddit, whatever — I'm there. But this leads us to the second level, which is interesting, at least I think so. We said: let's develop a plugin for Zoom. The plugin will know how to do one thing — it will show your engagement score.

I still don't know if it will be in real time or just at the end of the event, but we can show you — and we tested it — we can analyze the participants in the Zoom event and based on this create an engagement score. So you get: "Your engagement score is 86, and you are in the top 20% of the market. Want to know how to increase your engagement? Want to contact our team? Do you want us to tailor-fit a bespoke event with high engagement for you? We are here for you." We are actually in discussion with Zoom to understand what we can do so that they will promote us, or at least not create any problems for us.

And by the way, we found a way — I can tell you in advance — what's nice here is that I'm actually marketing a free piece of software. I will not even ask them to put in their credit card details, which is the most challenging part. I just want their email. Give me your email, you get this plugin — very easy to install. Usually the customer acquisition cost of free plugins is quite low. So we can actually do it, and it's relatively simple, frankly. Next week I can develop it, so it's something quite straightforward. Now, the Holy Grail — and this one I didn't have time to write up — is that we want to try and establish this as a metric for advertisers as well.

One of the biggest challenges of virtual events is finding sponsors. Everybody wants to find a sponsor, but there is no way for an advertiser to know the quality of the event. You told me 100 people came — first, how do I know? And second, what does it mean that they came? If I can tell them, "Hey, I have an engagement metric — my event scored 86," then suddenly the advertiser knows what to do with that, has something concrete in hand. So this is more or less the idea, and I'd value your feedback on it, because it's really fresh from the oven — we developed it over the weekend.

This is the engagement score of the meeting — the specific Zoom meeting — of each person, how engaged that person was.

Let me explain how we think it will work. So you are the speaker. You start the Zoom, people log into your Zoom.

Okay.

All right. So you can see everybody on the screen — remember, because you are the one in control. We will put a plugin that will go and check each of the participants. It will look at the camera and see: are you on camera or not on camera? Let's start with that. If you're on camera, are you looking at me, or are you looking down, or are you just walking around? So we can start doing the simpler thing — like a teacher. I look at you, I look at you, I look at you. I see everybody with their eyes closed — I know I'm losing them. If I see all of you looking at me, that's good. Basically, the most simple thing.

But we can also do it every 10 minutes, very easily. And we can start telling you, "Listen, you're losing your people."

We can also analyze the number of questions being asked, the texts being sent, the emoticons being sent, people leaving, people joining.

So you're scoring the meeting.

Yes.

The meeting.

Yes.

The meeting. Because this is very important also for the person hosting the event, who wants to know if people are focused or not — and if people are not focused, they want to know what to do to increase engagement. Now, I've done a search — there are 3,000 plugins for Zoom, and more or less the same number for Microsoft Teams. I found 10 plugins dealing with engagement. None of them gives an engagement score. All of them try to sell you engagement tools. So for that reason, I will not try to sell them engagement tools. I'm saying: if you want advice, call us. And probably this is something you mentioned in one of your lectures — make your product a service. So this is how I'm making my product a service.

And naturally, at the end, we want to funnel everybody into our system. We found a way to implement Zoom inside our system, so we are not competing with Zoom — because Zoom's rule is that they promote things that don't compete with them. So we'll try this.

What happens many times is you start building these tools and they take on a life of their own. You start thinking, "Wait, what else can I add to it?" And he started saying, "I can give you a tool for advertisers." So you can start offering something additional. Tools have a tendency to develop a life of their own, which is why they are so interesting. All right, we'll take a break. Thank you again, Oded. And then we'll go to the second part.

עודד נפחי: אוקיי, אז ננסה לדון במקרה הבוחן של Metaverse, החברה שאני מנהל כרגע. אני גם אראה לכם את המערכת שלנו, וגם אנסה לדון איתכם באתגרים — אולי יהיו לכם רעיונות טובים עבורנו. אז בואו נתחיל.

בדרך כלל אני אוהב להתייחס לסטארטאפים כסוג של טלנובלה. זה תמיד סיפור שבו מישהו אהב משהו, אז נבגד, אז אהב מישהו אחר, ואז גילו שהבת שאבדה נעלמה. כן, זה בעצם סטארטאפים.

במקרה שלנו, סיפור המקור של הסטארטאפ שלנו התחיל למעשה כחטיבה של חברה אחרת. הייתה חברה שנקראת AllSeated שפורבס אמרה שהמציאה את ה-Metaverse, והם גייסו הרבה כסף. העסק הבסיסי היה עיצוב אירועים — נניח שאתם רוצים לעשות בר מצווה, אתם באים לחברה הזו, הם מראים לכם את המקום, ואתם יכולים לבחור איזה שולחן, כיסא, או מה שתרצו באולם האירועים. אבל אז בא הקורונה, וכל חברות מארגני האירועים באו אליהם ואמרו, "היי, כבר יש לכם מודלים תלת-ממדיים של האולמות שלנו ואתם עובדים איתנו — בואו נעשה אירוע וירטואלי." זה הרגע שבו החברה פרחה. פורבס אמרה שהיא המציאה את ה-Metaverse לפני מארק צוקרברג, הם גייסו 20 מיליון דולר ללא כל קושי, והחיים היו מאוד טובים.

אבל אז הקורונה נגמרה. אז ברור היה להם שהם לא יכולים להמשיך לעשות את אותו הדבר, והם החליטו לסחרר את החברה החוצה. למה? כי עד שהם הכריזו על הפיצול והתחילו לנהל משא ומתן עם לקוחות פוטנציאליים, תוך כמה חודשים כבר אספו 15 לקוחות משלמים.

english_summary:
Metaverse, the company led by Oded Napchi, originated as a spin-out from AllSeated, an event-design firm that pivoted to virtual events during COVID-19, was dubbed by Forbes as an early Metaverse pioneer, and raised $20 million before the pandemic subsided. When Napchi joined as CEO, the company had 15 paying customers — including Fortune 500 names like Ferrero and Citizens Bank — but no clear understanding of why those customers had chosen them. The official positioning, "enterprise Metaverse," turned out to attract roughly 20 searches per year globally, making it essentially a non-market.

Napchi began by auditing the company's marketing operations. Pay-per-click advertising cost $7,500 per month and yielded one new customer every two months, translating to a $12,000 customer acquisition cost. An ABM (Account-Based Marketing) programme — effectively a rebranded cold-calling effort — cost $16,000 per month and produced only one customer in an entire year, prompting Napchi to eliminate the five-person team running it. The more revealing discovery came from interviewing existing customers: the majority, and the highest-value ones, were HR and Learning & Development departments using the platform primarily for employee training and onboarding. Customers explained that connecting new hires with colleagues during onboarding dramatically reduced early attrition — a compelling, concrete business outcome.

Rather than stopping at "HR training" as a niche, Napchi sought the broader category. Consulting industry veterans from Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and ON24, he identified a universal pain point: all major video-conferencing platforms lose audience engagement after roughly 40 minutes, yet many professional use cases — training, onboarding, medical education, webinars, and virtual sales events — demand sessions of 60 minutes or more. This became the company's new positioning: Metaverse sustains engagement for over three hours where standard platforms fail within one. The refined target audience shifted from large enterprise IT buyers to content marketing agencies, of which more than 20,000 operate in the United States alone.

To own the concept of "engagement" in the market's mind, the team is developing a free Zoom plugin that analyses participant behaviour — camera presence, eye contact, chat activity, reactions — and generates a real-time engagement score for meeting hosts. The plugin requires only an email to install, keeping acquisition costs low, while naturally funnelling interested users toward the full Metaverse platform. A further ambition is to offer this engagement score to event sponsors, giving advertisers an objective quality metric that currently does not exist in the virtual events industry. The broader lesson Napchi draws is one familiar to any startup founder: a great product without sharp marketing will go unnoticed, and finding the right market framing — through customer interviews, search-volume analysis, and expert consultation — is often more valuable than any product feature.

הרצאה זו מציגה מקרה בוחן אמיתי של סטארטאפ בשם Metaverse, שהנחיל עודד נפחי — יזם ומנהל בעל ניסיון רב. הסטארטאפ צמח מתוך חטיבה של חברת AllSeated, שסיפקה עיצוב אירועים תלת-ממדי ופרחה בתקופת הקורונה בזכות מעבר לאירועים וירטואליים. עם סיום המגפה, החברה הופרדה לישות עצמאית עם 15 לקוחות משלמים, חלקם מרשימת Fortune 500 — אך ללא הבנה ברורה מה בדיוק הם מוכרים ולמי.

הנחי מצא כי ה-positioning המקורי — "Enterprise Metaverse" — לא נתמך בביקוש: כ-20 חיפושים בלבד בשנה. בנוסף, ערוץ השיווק העיקרי, ABM (שיחות קרות ממותגות), הניב מעל 100 לידים בחודש אך לקוח בודד בשנה בעלות של 16,000 דולר — כישלון מסחרי מובהק שהוביל לפיטורי חמישה עובדים. מניתוח הלקוחות הקיימים עלה כי רוב הלקוחות המשמעותיים עסקו בהדרכה ו-Learning & Development. ראיונות עומק חשפו את הצורך האמיתי: חברות ביקשו להוריד תחלופת עובדים על ידי טיפוח קשרים חברתיים עוד בשלב ה-onboarding, ואת כך הפלטפורמה אפשרה בצורה ייחודית.

מיצוב מחדש סביב בעיית שחיקת העובדים הוביל לתוצאות מרשימות: עלות רכישת לקוח צנחה מ-12,000 ל-2,500 דולר, מחזור המכירות התקצר מחצי שנה לחודשיים, ותוצאות השיווק הוכפלו תוך קיצוץ תקציב לשליש. ואולם, גם עם ה-positioning החדש, נפח החיפוש נותר מוגבל — כ-100 חיפושים בחודש — רחוק מלהוות בסיס לעסק בר-קיימא.

כדי להרחיב את השוק, נפחי פנה למומחי תעשייה לשעבר מחברות כגון Zoom ו-Teams, שהצביעו על בעיה אוניברסלית: פלטפורמות וידאו מאבדות engagement לאחר 40 דקות. ה-USP החדש גובש בפשטות: 75% ממשתמשי ועידות הווידאו מאבדים מיקוד לאחר שעה, בעוד הפלטפורמה שומרת על engagement של יותר משלוש שעות. מנוע השיווק שנבחר כ-beachhead מתמקד ב-content marketing agencies, תוך גישה יצירתית דרך קהילות גיימינג ברדיט — קהל שחשוף לפורמטים דיגיטליים ועשוי להיחשף באופן אורגני לפלטפורמה.

יוזמה נוספת שפותחה לאחרונה היא plugin ל-Zoom שמודד engagement score בזמן אמת — ניתוח תשומת הלב של משתתפים דרך המצלמה, כמות שאלות, הודעות ואמוג'ים — ומציע למנחים פידבק מעשי. הכלי מתוכנן להיות גשר שיוביל משתמשים לפלטפורמה המלאה, מבלי להתחרות ישירות ב-Zoom. ההרצאה ממחישה עיקרון מרכזי: marketing איכותי עולה על product מושלם, וזיהוי מדויק של ה-use case האמיתי — לעיתים על ידי פנייה למומחי תעשייה ולא רק ללקוחות — הוא המפתח להפיכת רעיון לעסק.
